market_context: United States/general English; USDA/FDA date-labeling rules with EU distinction explained where relevant
title: Use-by vs. best-before dates: what do they actually mean?

seo.title: Use-by vs. best-before food dates explained
seo.meta_description: In the U.S., most food dates are quality labels, not federal safety deadlines. 'Best if used by,' 'sell by' and 'use by' do not have one universal meaning; infant formula is an exception.
seo.search_intent: Understand what common food date labels mean in the United States and how they differ from EU use-by rules.

excerpt: In the United States, most package dates are about quality rather than a federally defined safety deadline. 'Best if Used By' signals peak quality; 'Sell-By' helps store inventory; and 'Use-By' is generally a manufacturer's quality recommendation, with infant formula a key regulated exception. This differs from the EU, where a use-by date on highly perishable food is a safety limit.
content_html:
American food dates are confusing partly because the same phrase does not carry the legal meaning that a European shopper might expect. Except for infant formula, federal law generally does not make package dates a universal food-safety cutoff.

Common U.S. phraseTypical meaning
Best if Used By/BeforePeak flavor or quality
Sell-ByRetail inventory guidance
Use-ByManufacturer's recommended peak-quality date in most foods
Freeze-ByDate suggested for freezing to preserve quality

A refrigerated ready-to-eat food and a dry box of pasta may both carry voluntary dates, but in the U.S. the wording alone usually does not create a federal safety deadline. Storage time, temperature and product-specific handling guidance still determine whether a perishable food is safe.

Infant formula is a real exception

FDA requires a “Use By” date on infant formula. Do not use formula after that date because the manufacturer guarantees nutrient content and acceptable quality only through the stated date.

A date does not replace safe storage

Food kept too warm can become unsafe before a quality date. Conversely, a properly handled shelf-stable product may remain wholesome after a “Best if Used By” date if there are no signs of spoilage or package damage.

Why advice online seems contradictory

In the European Union, “use by” on highly perishable food is specifically a safety date: food should not be eaten after it even if it smells normal. U.S. “Use-By” wording usually does not carry that same universal legal definition.

Date wording is a risk-management tool, not a universal freshness test. A use-by date is normally attached to foods where safety can become a concern even when smell or appearance seem normal. That is why tasting the product to “check” it is not a sensible strategy once the date has passed. Best-before dates mainly describe expected quality under proper storage.

Freezing can pause the clock for many foods if it happens while the food is still within its safe period. Once frozen, texture may change, but microbial growth is largely halted. After thawing, the product should be handled according to normal refrigerated-food rules rather than assuming the original date no longer matters at all.

Opened packaging is another important distinction. A carton, jar, deli pack, or ready-to-eat food may carry a date that applies to the unopened product, while the label separately says to consume within a certain number of days after opening. That shorter instruction often becomes the relevant one.

Common sense still matters for best-before foods. Dry goods, canned products, crackers, coffee, and similar items may remain usable after the quality date if the package is intact and storage has been appropriate. Changes such as mold, insects, swollen packaging, leaks, or obvious spoilage override the printed date.

Temperature history can be more important than the printed date. A refrigerated food left in a hot car for hours may become unsafe before its use-by date, while the same product kept continuously cold follows the intended shelf-life conditions. Dates assume the storage instructions on the label have been respected.

Retail markdowns near a use-by date can still be useful if the food will be cooked, eaten, or frozen promptly. The key is to plan rather than buy discounted perishables and forget them at the back of the refrigerator. A date is most useful when combined with good stock rotation at home.

Best-before foods can also lose different qualities at different rates. Cereal may become stale, spices lose aroma, chocolate develop bloom, and coffee taste flat without necessarily becoming unsafe. Quality decline is often gradual rather than a sudden switch at midnight on the printed date.

Household organization prevents many date-related mistakes. Put newer products behind older ones, write the opening date on jars or cartons when the label gives an after-opening limit, and freeze items before they become urgent. These habits reduce waste without asking smell or appearance to answer safety questions they cannot reliably answer.

When in doubt about a safety date on a highly perishable food, following the label is the safer choice than trying to stretch it for a small saving.

The practical rule

Read the phrase next to the date, follow refrigeration instructions, and do not use a quality date as permission to ignore time and temperature. For U.S. infant formula, follow the Use By date strictly.

faq.question: Is food unsafe after the Best if Used By date?
faq.answer: Not automatically. USDA describes that phrase as a quality indicator, assuming the food has been handled properly.

faq.question: Is Use-By always a safety date in the U.S.?
faq.answer: No. For most U.S. foods it is a quality recommendation; infant formula is a regulated exception.
